articles.title: US army major claims Pentagon ignored warnings over Kuwait base security before Iranian drone strike killed 6 troops in March
articles.summary: A whistleblower Army Major alleges the Pentagon ignored repeated warnings about inadequate security at a Kuwait base prior to a drone strike that killed six US troops, raising serious concerns about military preparedness and leadership accountability.
articles.body: US military officials were warned that an Army command post in Kuwait lacked adequate protection against Iranian drone attacks before a strike killed six American service members on March 1, according to a whistleblower complaint submitted to Congress cited by CBS News. Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who survived the attack on the Port Shuaiba facility, alleged that concerns about the site's security were raised with senior military leadership but not addressed before the strike. He described the incident as “a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself, all the way down to my level” in an interview with CBS News' 60 Minutes.Ramsbottom, who served as deputy chief of operations for the Army Reserve's 103rd Sustainment Command, submitted the complaint to the House and Senate Armed Services committees on Friday. He said the facility had been designed to withstand ground-based threats but lacked the infrastructure needed to defend against aerial attacks.“It was designed to stop car bombs and threats like that. There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack,” he told 60 Minutes.The March 1 drone strike targeted a tactical operations centre at Port Shuaiba during the opening days of Operation Epic Fury. It killed six US service members: Army Reserve Capt. Cody Khork, 35; Sgt. 1st Class Noah Tietjens, 42; Sgt. 1st Class Nicole Amor, 39; Sgt. Declan Coady, 20; Maj. Jeffrey O’Brien, 45; and Chief Warrant Officer Three Robert Marzan, 54.Ramsbottom said he had raised concerns about the lack of protection with Maj. Gen. John Hinson, the officer responsible for logistics at US Central Command (CENTCOM).“I brought it up twice in various meetings, basically saying, 'Hey, I don’t see how we’re protected here,'” he said.According to Ramsbottom, Hinson responded: “We don’t have to worry about protection.”The major also alleged that personnel at Port Shuaiba had requested a counter-drone defence system but were told the Pentagon would attempt to provide one. However, he said the equipment never reached the facility.“It never arrived at Shuaiba,” Ramsbottom said. “And we don’t know if it was ever even ordered or requested.”His complaint also highlighted gaps in emergency medical facilities, alleging that the site had no physician, no permanent aid station and only one ambulance.The allegations contrast with statements made by senior US defence officials following the attack. War Secretary Pete Hegseth said Port Shuaiba had been protected but acknowledged that a drone had managed to penetrate the defences.“Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through,” Hegseth told reporters the day after the strike. He said the drone struck a fortified tactical operations centre, adding that such weapons could cause significant damage.Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell also rejected claims about the facility's security. In a March 3 post on X, he disputed CBS News' reporting, saying the tactical operations centre was not a makeshift office.“This ‘reporting’ from CBS is not true,” Parnell wrote, adding that the facility had been reinforced with six-foot walls.You use AI every day. articles.title: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
articles.summary: The Estonian government says Russia was behind the attempted sabotage, which the Kremlin denies.
articles.body:
Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".

The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.

They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.

On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.

The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.

Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.

The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.

Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.

One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.

Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."

Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.

Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.

Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

articles.title: 'I felt accepted': Sonia Gandhi revisits 2004 Cong win, opens up at memoir launch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: At the launch of her memoir, Sonia Gandhi recalled the Congress victory in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections as the moment she felt accepted in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At the launch of her memoir, Sonia Gandhi recalled the Congress victory in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections as the moment she felt accepted in India. She said her first sense of belonging came when people in her husband Rajiv Gandhi's constituency accepted her.According to PTI, Sonia Gandhi said the 2004 election victory marked an important moment in her journey, while recalling how she gradually found acceptance in India. She also spoke about her relationship with former prime minister Indira Gandhi and the impact of Rajiv Gandhi's assassination on her family."I felt accepted when Congress won in 2004," Sonia Gandhi said, recalling the party's victory as a significant moment in her personal and political journey. She added that her first feeling of belonging came when she visited Rajiv Gandhi's constituency and people accepted her.Speaking about her relationship with former prime minister Indira Gandhi, Sonia said she was in awe of her formidable personality and initially felt intimidated by her."I was in awe of Indira Gandhi; she was formidable, I was scared of her," she said. Sonia added that she learnt discipline, punctuality, courage and determination from Indira Gandhi.Explaining why she decided to write the memoir, Sonia said she wanted to counter what she believes are inaccurate accounts about her life. "One reason I chose to write the book is so much is being said and most of it is so unreal," she said.Reacting to the response to the book, she added, "Response to the book has been overwhelming, I'm deeply touched."Recalling the period after Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991, Sonia spoke about how family roles changed. She said Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra became her emotional support after their father's death."I became the child, Rahul, Priyanka became parents after Rajiv's death," she said.Speaking about political participation, Sonia urged more young people to enter politics and take an active role in public life."I feel more young people should come forward and join politics," she said.Sonia Gandhi's book, Belonging: A Journey of Love, offers insights into her personal life, her relationship with the Nehru-Gandhi family and the experiences that shaped her political journey.The book launch saw the presence of several prominent political figures, including Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.Opposition leaders such as Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and National Conference president Farooq Abdullah also attended the event, along with former vice-president Hamid Ansari and other political leaders.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Grammys 2027: Raye leads with 11 nominations as Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods
articles.summary: British singer Raye lands 11 nominations while Dolly Parton is recognised two months after her death.
articles.body:
British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumous nods.

Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.

Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.

Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.

Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.

The late country star also received a nomination for best audio book, for her narration of Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.

The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.

That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.

Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.

Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

There are five new categories being introduced, including best Latin song and best Asian pop music performance.

They have been added as part of the Academy's attempts to make the event "more inclusive" and represent a wider range of music genres.

However, critics fear that the new specialist categories will result in genres such as K-pop being under-represented in the major categories, and acts including BTS and Stray Kids have said they will boycott next year's ceremony.

Four of Korea’s five biggest entertainment companies withheld their music from consideration. Starship Entertainment, which bucked the trend, scored nominations for its girl bands IVE and KiiiKiii.

The other nominees were Babymetal, Japanese singer Lisa (not to be confused with the Blackpink star of the same name) and the Filipino bands BINI and SB19.

Elsewhere, Beyoncé picked up the 100th nomination of her career when Morning Dew (Donk) was shortlisted for best R&B solo performance.

Songs and albums had to be released between 31 August 2025 and 28 August 2026 to qualify for nominations.

Around 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy are eligible to vote for the winners.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial for deaths of her three children in March 2027
articles.summary: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.

The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.

Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges, the same as originally filed.

She is accused of strangling five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan at the family home on 24 January 2023, but the defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.

Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges.

The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.

A week ago, Judge William Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.

Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.

The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.

Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.

It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.

The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.

The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.

Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Bahrain court sentences dozens of Shia Muslims to life in prison, activists say
articles.summary:
Most of those jailed on Iran-linked terrorism charges are clerics, a UK-based human rights group, claiming confessions were forced.

Bahraini authorities accused the 69 unnamed defendants of establishing a terrorist group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
articles.body:
Sixty-four Shia Muslims, most of them clerics, have been sentenced to life in prison in Bahrain on Iran-linked terrorism charges, according to a UK-based human rights group.

The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) said another five people were handed 15-year prison sentences by the High Criminal Court in Manama.

The advocate general confirmed the sentences but did not give the number of defendants or identify them. He said they were accused of establishing a terrorist group linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

BIRD condemned the verdicts, saying there had been "credible allegations of torture, coerced confessions, and severe restrictions on the defence".

Authorities in the Sunni Muslim-ruled kingdom have reportedly detained hundreds of people, most of them members of its Shia majority, on suspicion of espionage and terrorism offences since the start of the US and Israel's war with regional Shia power Iran in February.

Dozens have also been stripped of their Bahraini citizenship after being accused by the government of "sympathy and praise for Iran's hostile and criminal acts".

Iran has launched thousands of missiles and drones at Bahrain and other Gulf Arab states hosting US forces during the war. On Sunday, the Bahraini military said it had intercepted "several Iranian aerial attacks".

Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

Fifty-six of the defendants sentenced on Monday were arrested in May and June.

BIRD said 47 of them were Shia clerics - including Sheikh Mohammed Sanqour and Sheikh Ali al-Sadadi, who led Friday prayers at the Imam al-Sadiq Grand Mosque in Duraz, and Sayed Moosa al-Alwedaie, who served as imam at the Grand Mosque in Ras Rumman - and nine were their affiliates, including religious reciters.

The 13 other defendants - including the exiled cleric Sheikh Isa Qassim, who holds the religious rank of ayatollah and ​is widely regarded as the spiritual ​leader of Bahrain's Shia community - were tried in absentia, it said. Bahraini authorities said most of them were in Iran.

The 64 defendants faced charges including establishing a terrorist group, which the Public Prosecution said was linked to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), and calling for the suspension of the provisions of the constitution and a change in the system of government.

The prosecution alleged that they had incited terrorist acts and promoted "Velayat-e Faqih" (rule by the supreme jurist), which is the backbone of Iran's theocratic system.

The High Criminal Court convicted all the defendants and imposed prison sentences ranging from 15 years to life, the advocate general and head of the Terrorist Crimes Prosecution announced . The court also fined some of the defendants $265,000 (£200,000) and ordered the confiscation of $21.2m (£16m) for charitable purposes.

The director of BIRD, Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, said the verdicts were "deeply unjust" and constituted "an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain's Shia community".

Reuters news agency cited a person close to the clerics' defence teams as describing the sentences as "worse than anything we imagined".

Last week, BIRD, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International were among 20 human rights groups which signed an open letter calling on Bahraini authorities to investigate what they described as "serious allegations of torture" in the case.

They said defendants had reported being "subjected to forced standing, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, sleep deprivation, and threats of physical and sexual violence against themselves and their families, as well as citizenship revocation and deportation". Many were pressured to sign lengthy statements they were not allowed to read, they added.

The advocate general insisted on Monday that all the defendants' legal rights had been guaranteed during the investigation and that they had been given a fair trial.

articles.title: Police officers lied about searches connected to fatal St Mellons crash, hearing told
articles.summary: PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone face gross misconduct allegations over their actions.
articles.body:
Two police officers lied about carrying out missing person searches at the homes of two young women who were involved in a triple fatal crash, a police misconduct hearing has heard.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone face gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in a woodland in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

The two serving Gwent officers attended the hearing and denied all allegations against them.

The hearing before a panel being held at Rodney Parade heard that Smith, Darcy Ross and Russon had been friends for years and went out together in Newport on 2 March 2023.

They met three men, Rafel Jeanne, Shane Loughlin and Joel Lia, with the six eventually travelling to a caravan in Trecco Bay, Porthcawl, for a party.

Barrister Stephen Morley, for Gwent Police's professional standards department, which is bringing the case, said the group then left in the early hours, with the car coming off the road shortly after the group had dropped off one passenger in Cardiff.

By the evening of Saturday, 3 March, the families of the three young women "were so worried that they decided to report them missing to Gwent Police", having been unable to contact them for hours and noting their lack of presence on social media

Ross's mother, Claire Ross, and Russon's father, Nathan Russon, went to Newport central police station to report their children missing.

The panel was told logs were created at this time which would help with subsequent enquiries.

During this time, Smith's mother, Emma Borg, had gone to the caravan the young people had travelled to and found her daughter's handbag there but no sign of the group.

Morley told the hearing that the "people in the caravan weren't particularly helpful", making Smith's mother realise that "something was very wrong".

Smith was eventually reported missing by her sister Lauren Doyle a couple of hours later, which included "sensitive information" adding overall to what was described as a "very worrying set of circumstances".

He added that the force also received "some concerning information about the men that was added to the system" which he said he would not read out in public.

The hearing was told that PC Hardwick and PC Livingstone were on a 16:00 to 03:00 shift and were given the "straightforward task of attending two home addresses to take any details from family members and to search".

Morley said this was something that "should always happen" during a missing person's enquiry and was "common sense" - allowing officers to assess whether the missing person might actually be at home, might have left something of importance behind like a note or might have taken something of importance.

The panel heard PC Livingstone had been assigned the search of Smith's house and PC Hardwick that of Russon's, but the two officers went to both addresses together and when they returned filled in the relevant paperwork.

PC Livingstone said she had first spoken to Smith's brother and then her mother.

In relation to the search, the following was written down: "Nothing missing out of the usual.

"Mum and Dad was concerned and Mum believed she went out in the same clothes and has not taken any new clothes with her."

That, the panel were told, was a "dishonest and misleading entry".

PC Hardwick was said to have written in the log relating to Russon.

He wrote "Premise search conducted" - words that the panel heard "really speaks for itself - our case is that is dishonest".

Subsequent statements from the two women's families said no searches had taken place, with Russon's father saying he would not have allowed the police to search his daughter's bedroom.

Morley said it was for the panel to decide whether there could be any confusion over the families' accounts, adding there was "no reason to doubt" the evidence provided by the families.

The hearing was told PC Hardwick and PC Livingstone were said to have updated one of the officers overseeing the investigation, Sgt Cheverton, that the searches had taken place.

The panel heard that while the two officers' actions "may not have made any difference" in relation to the outcome for the occupants of the car, Morley said that was "neither here nor there, as these officers are expected do a proper job".

Two other officers were assigned the search of Ross's house and it was agreed that a "search of some sorts" had happened there.

By August 2023, the police watchdog was investigating Gwent Police's response to the missing person's reports and, in a statement to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), PC Hardwick denied the allegations and said he did search the bedroom of Russon.

PC Livingstone also gave an interview to the IOPC saying she had not "knowingly been untruthful in her accounts" but added that, given the passage of time, she could not remember whether searches had taken place.

If gross misconduct is proven against either officer then they would be dismissed without notice from the force.

The hearing is expected to last until the end of the week.

articles.title: Bo French won’t bo-w out: MAGA hardliner continues to bait Indian immigrants despite Texas rout
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: Losing an election by nearly 700,000 votes would ordinarily be considered an emphatic hint from the electorate to take
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Losing an election by nearly 700,000 votes would ordinarily be considered an emphatic hint from the electorate to take up gardening or fishing or some other stress-relieving hobby. Not for Bo French.The defeated Republican MAGA candidate for Texas railroad commissioner appears to have decided that if voters won't give him a public office, he can at least keep himself employed as a full-time provocateur on social media, pushing ahead with his snide attacks on Indian-Americans with posts on who qualifies as a “real American,” this time by using his family tree as the admission ticket. It was French’s broadside against Indian immigrants that was widely seen as inviting the rout of the GOP in Texas in mid-term elections.Having ceded 32 years of Republican control of the Texas railroad commission -- the powerful body that regulates the state’s oil and gas industry despite its misleading name -- in addition to losing the governorship and a Senate seat, French resumed his immigrant-baiting last week as if liberated him from the tiresome business of seeking votes."As an American, who's family has been here for 400 years, I shouldn't have to listen to people who are in fact not from here, do not share our culture, scam our institutions, and hate our nation, because they shouldn't be here in the first place," he posted on X, after moderate Republicans blamed his attacks on Indian-Americans for the GOP rout in Texas, where Democrats have captured almost every office after decades.The post attracted a piercing response from Harmeet Dhillon, a fellow Republican and till recently head of the justice department's civil rights division who resigned last week, apparently realizing she was not on the same page as MAGA extremists."Whose," she began, correcting French’s English after deciding if was going to lecture America about heritage, he could at least try to master the language inherited from his ancestors. "Also, you are an ignorant bigot whose racist rhetoric helped turn off many Americans from voting Republican in Texas. You should do the party a favor and disappear from public life. This is MY party and country as much as it is anyone's," she wrote.French reeled back, clarifying that Dhillon was not the person he was talking about, and the problem was not immigrants generally, but “immigrants who scam institutions and hate America.” But other moderate Republicans jumped in, reminding French that being Republican does not require passing an ancestry test administered by a man named Bo who cost the party Texas and possibly beyond."You were a ball and chain wrapped around the necks of the GOP in Texas. You can take credit for the worst GOP losses in TX for decades. We don't do hierarchies of Americans," wrote Nebraska Republican Don Bacon. French reeled back some more, thanking Bacon for his military service, but he subsequently declared: "There are few people more uppity than RINOs" -- Trump and MAGA shorthand for Republicans in Name Only, a category for conservatives who disagree with hardliners.More Republicans joined the grammatical firing squad as moderates in the party appeared to rediscover their mojo. "Ok well in 400 years you couldn't learn proper English grammar...?" sneered congressman Dan Crenshaw asked, while Conservative commentator Marc Thiessen offered a more historical correction. “1620s? Wow. So you’re descended from boat people who were the rid-raff of 17th century Europe and came here seeking a better life. Congratulations you’re no different than anyone else here,” he wrote.French still has his hardline supporters, one of whom declared there was "nothing controversial about this statement," arguing that conservative commentators attacking French were merely exposing their own discomfort, while another celebrated his promise that Republicans like Dhillon would be replaced by "patriots". French continued to accuse his critics of wanting to replace Americans with foreigners and insisted that he was highlighting alleged H-1B visa fraud and unfair treatment of Texas residents in university admissions.Still pinned on his account was the idea that that if implemented would reduce the US population by around 30 per cent. "We have 100 million people in this country who shouldn't be here. They don't share our values. They don't want to assimilate....We have to send them all home. It is the only way we are going to save our country and our culture.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
